The maximum total length observed in wild populations of the Spearsnouted grenadier, Coelorinchus labiatus, reaches 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters]. This size represents the terminal somatic dimension achieved by the species in its deep-sea habitat, a value that is characteristic of many macrourids and reflects the constraints of a cold, food-limited environment on somatic growth. Recent comparative analyses within the Macrouridae family suggest that this ultimate body size is intermediate between smaller-bodied congeners and larger macrourids such as Coryphaenoides rupestris. Growth trajectories derived from otolith readings indicate that the species undergoes a prolonged period of somatic expansion, which is typical of deep-water teleosts inhabiting cold, food-limited environments.

The total length at which individuals attain puberty has been established at 21 centimeters [Lp = 21 centimeters]. This measurement was inferred from anatomical examination of gonadal development in a series of specimens collected during research trawls across the North Atlantic. The onset of gonad maturation at this body size implies that the species begins diverting resources toward reproductive effort well before reaching its asymptotic length. By comparison, related macrourids often exhibit a similar relationship between length at maturity and ultimate size, suggesting a conserved pattern of life-history timing within the subfamily.

Newly emerged prolarvae carry a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0092 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0092 grams]. This remarkably low neonatal mass is consistent with the production of small, yolk-laden pelagic eggs that drift in deep-water currents until hatching. The initial weight dictates an early reliance on endogenous reserves, and the yolk-sac larva must absorb its nutrients before transitioning to active feeding on microzooplankton. The small size at emergence imposes a tight energetic budget during the initial period of exogenous nutrition, when mouth gape opening and retinal differentiation must occur rapidly to enable first prey capture.

The wet weight at puberty for this grenadier has been calculated as 41.4 grams [Wwp = 41.4 grams]. This mass corresponds to the length at maturity and represents the body condition at which the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully activated. Individuals reaching this mass are capable of vitellogenesis and spermiation onset, marking the initiation of active spawning cycles. The weight gain from the post-settlement juvenile phase to this pubertal threshold is substantial, reflecting the energetic costs of building the somatic framework required for sustained reproduction in the cold, dark waters of the continental slope. The ultimate wet weight recorded in fully grown adults is 660 grams [Wwi = 660 grams], more than fifteen times the weight at puberty. This extraordinary growth capacity underscores the potential for extensive post-maturation somatic investment.

Under the consistent thermal regime of the deep-water habitat, which averages 6.7 °C [T = 6.7 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Spearsnouted grenadier is estimated at ten years [am = ten years]. This longevity is longer than that of many shallow-water teleosts of equivalent size, a pattern frequently linked to the reduced metabolic demands and slower aging rates observed in cold-adapted fishes. Under these same thermal conditions, females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate yielding approximately 6,500 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 6,500 eggs per spawning event] and a spawning frequency of one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year]. This high fecundity per event is thought to compensate for elevated egg and larval mortality in the pelagic environment, ensuring that enough progeny survive to recruit into the adult population.
